## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Mathematical Methods for Neuroscience
  Official title       Méthodes mathématiques pour les neurosciences
  Instructors          R. VELTZ, Q.CORMIER (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 40 h (lectures 24 h, tutorials 16 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track Santé]{.badge .track}
  Language             Not displayed on master-mva.com or on the Université Paris-Saclay page (the master-mva.com description is written in French)
  Assessment           Exam for the first session; resit in the form of a paper reading (master-mva.com, “Mode de validation”) · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment) · no weighting displayed
  Prerequisites        Mathematics at the level of L3 and M1 courses (master-mva.com, “Prè-requis”)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, physics or computer science who wants to see how dynamical systems, bifurcation theory and stochastic processes become quantitative models of neurons and of the cortex.

**Empirical first**: inject a constant current into the Hodgkin–Huxley model of the squid giant axon. Up to about 6 µA/cm² the membrane stays at rest; just above, it fires repetitively at about 55 Hz, and never at 5 Hz. Why can the firing rate not start from zero, why do many cortical neurons do the opposite, and why do the geometric hallucinations reported under mescaline so often look like tunnels, funnels, spirals and lattices?

Each of these questions has a precise mathematical answer, and this course builds the tools that give it. Single neurons are low-dimensional dynamical systems whose behaviour changes at bifurcations; noise turns them into diffusion processes with first-passage times; large networks are described by neural fields and by mean-field limits, in which symmetry dictates which spatial patterns appear. The course is taught by Romain Veltz and Quentin Cormier (INRIA, per master-mva.com). It shares its stochastic tools with [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) and its random-matrix tools with [Large Random Matrices and Applications to Machine Learning](../s2-random-matrices-ml/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Write, simulate and analyse the space-clamped Hodgkin–Huxley model and its reductions (FitzHugh–Nagumo, integrate-and-fire, quadratic integrate-and-fire).
-   Draw the phase portrait of a planar system, find its equilibria, invariant manifolds and limit cycles, and decide their stability.
-   State and use Hartman–Grobman, the topological classification of hyperbolic equilibria, structural stability and the centre manifold theorem.
-   Recognise saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations, reduce a system to its normal form and compute the first Lyapunov coefficient.
-   Explain the two classical excitability classes of neurons through the bifurcation that creates firing.
-   Solve linear stochastic differential equations, write the Fokker–Planck equation and compute mean first-passage times and the firing rate of a noisy integrate-and-fire neuron.
-   Describe the anatomy and functional architecture of the primary visual cortex and model it with neural field equations.
-   Use symmetry (O(2) and the Euclidean group) to predict orientation tuning, cortical patterns and the geometry of visual hallucinations.
-   Derive the dynamic mean-field equations of random rate networks and the transition to chaos.
-   Prove propagation of chaos for interacting diffusions by coupling, and derive the mean-field limits of spiking networks and of neural masses.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: mathematics at the level of L3 and M1 courses. In practice, the course uses ordinary differential equations, linear algebra, Fourier series and measure-theoretic probability.

-   **Preparation** — the refreshers [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (eigenvalues, matrix exponential, implicit function theorem), [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (Gaussian vectors, conditional expectation, limit theorems) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (the simulations of this page). Chapter 0 reviews what is used.
-   **Related courses in the same semester** — [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) develops Itô calculus and the links between diffusions and partial differential equations in depth; [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) studies the Wasserstein distances behind propagation of chaos; [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html) studies the non-convex optimisation of neural networks, to which the mean-field tools of ch. 8 apply (ch. 9.5); [Medical Image Analysis Based on Generative, Geometric and Biophysical Models](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html) is another Santé-track course of the same semester.
-   **Courses that build on it or share its tools (semester 2)** — [Functional Brain Imaging and Brain–Computer Interfaces](../s2-brain-imaging-bci/index.html) (the signals that neural masses model), [Large Random Matrices and Applications to Machine Learning](../s2-random-matrices-ml/index.html) (the random-matrix tools behind ch. 7), [Interactions: Complexity, Stochasticity, Extrema and Rare Events](../s2-interactions/index.html) (interacting particle systems, chaos and rare events) and [Stopping Times and Online Algorithms](../s2-stopping-times-online/index.html) (stopping times, of which the first-passage times of ch. 4 are an example).

### Course outline

-   **Review: differential equations, Fourier analysis and probability** — existence and uniqueness, Grönwall, linear systems, convolution and Fourier modes, Gaussian tools.
-   **Neuron models** — the membrane circuit, the Hodgkin–Huxley equations, their reductions, synapses and the cable equation.
-   **Dynamical systems** — phase portraits, invariant manifolds, equivalence, Hartman–Grobman, structural stability and the centre manifold.
-   **Bifurcation theory** — saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations, normal forms, excitability classes and equivariant bifurcations.
-   **The role of noise** — Brownian motion, Itô calculus, Fokker–Planck equations and the firing rate of noisy neurons.
-   **The visual cortex and neural field models** — the anatomy and functional architecture of V1, the Amari equation, bumps, Turing patterns and fronts.
-   **Symmetry in V1** — orientation tuning in the ring model, cortical patterns on lattices and the geometry of visual hallucinations.
-   **Mean-field theory I** — random rate networks, the circular law, dynamic mean-field theory and the transition to chaos, the Ben Arous–Guionnet theorem.
-   **Mean-field theory II** — McKean–Vlasov processes, propagation of chaos, mean-field limits of spiking networks and neural masses.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — mean-field models with spikes, numerical bifurcation analysis, structured random networks (self-study).

### Session plan {#sessions}

**40 h in class = 8 sessions of 5 h (3 h lecture + 2 h tutorial).** The volume is the Université Paris-Saclay programme table (24 h of lectures, 16 h of tutorials). Master-mva.com organises the course on Thursdays at ENS Paris-Saclay, with a lecture from 13:30 to 16:30 followed by a tutorial from 16:30 to 18:30, which gives exactly eight such afternoons. The split of the content into sessions is a proposal.

The order differs from the official list in one respect: neuron models (official item 5) come first, because they supply the examples of dynamical systems and bifurcations, and the visual cortex (official items 1 and 4) comes after the bifurcation theory it uses. Level 1 = foundations, 2 = core results, 3 = advanced and research-level material; it never decreases.

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session, even quickly: Grönwall's lemma and the Fourier modes of convolutions return in almost every chapter.
-   Run every code block. Each one checks a formula of the text against a simulation (the Hodgkin–Huxley f–I curve, the Siegert formula, the Turing wavelength, the width of the ring-model bump, the variance predicted by dynamic mean-field theory).
-   After each session, do the exercises listed in the session plan before reading on: ch. 3 relies on ch. 2, ch. 6 on ch. 3 and ch. 5, ch. 8 on ch. 4.
-   Keep a notebook of the normal forms of ch. 3: the same five equations organise ch. 1, ch. 5 and ch. 6.
-   The Python environment is NumPy and SciPy only; every simulation runs in a few seconds on a laptop.
-   The resit is a paper reading: the paper-study projects below are good training for it.

## 0. Review: differential equations, Fourier analysis and probability {#ch0}

Neuron and network models are differential equations: sometimes in finite dimension, sometimes on a space of functions, sometimes driven by noise. This chapter collects the M1-level results that the later chapters use without stopping: well-posedness, Grönwall's lemma, linear stability, the Fourier modes of convolution operators and a few Gaussian identities.

### 0.1 Existence, uniqueness and Grönwall's lemma

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — Cauchy–Lipschitz (Picard–Lindelöf)]{.tag} Let $E$ be a Banach space ($\mathbb{R}^n$, or a space of functions as in ch. 5) and $f : E \to E$ Lipschitz on every bounded set. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ this is the same as locally Lipschitz. For every $x_0 \in E$, the problem
$$
x' = f(x), \qquad x(0) = x_0
$$
has a unique maximal solution, defined on an interval $[0, T^*)$.

It is the unique continuous solution of the integral equation
$$
x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t f(x(s))\, ds .
$$

Blow-up alternative: if $T^* < \infty$, then $\|x(t)\| \to \infty$ as $t \to T^*$.

::: proof
*Existence*. On the ball $B$ of radius $r$ around $x_0$, $f$ is bounded by $M$ and $L$-Lipschitz.

The Picard map $\Phi(x)(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t f(x(s))\,ds$ sends $C([0, \delta], B)$ into itself when $\delta M \le r$.

It is a contraction for the sup norm when $\delta L < 1$, so the Banach fixed-point theorem gives a local solution.

*Uniqueness* follows from Lemma 0.2 below applied to the difference of two solutions.

*Blow-up alternative*. The existence step gives a time $\delta(R) > 0$ that depends only on the bounds $M$ and $L$ of $f$ on the ball of radius $2R$.

So from any starting point of norm at most $R$, the solution lives at least for a time $\delta(R)$.

Suppose $T^* < \infty$ and $\|x(t_k)\| \le R$ along a sequence $t_k \to T^*$. Restarting from $x(t_k)$ with $T^* - t_k < \delta(R)$ extends the solution beyond $T^*$, contradicting maximality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Lemma 0.2 — Grönwall]{.tag} Let $u \ge 0$ be continuous on $[0, T]$ and $a, b \ge 0$ with $u(t) \le a + b \int_0^t u(s)\,ds$ for all $t$. Then
$$
u(t) \le a\, e^{bt}, \qquad 0 \le t \le T .
$$

::: proof
Let $v(t) = a + b \int_0^t u$. Then $v' = b u \le b v$, so $(v e^{-bt})' \le 0$ and $v(t) \le a e^{bt}$. Conclude with $u \le v$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Applied to two solutions of $x' = f(x)$ with $f$ globally $L$-Lipschitz, it gives the continuous dependence on initial data used in ch. 4, ch. 5 and ch. 8:
$$
\|x(t) - y(t)\| \le \|x(0) - y(0)\|\, e^{Lt}.
$$
::::

### 0.2 Linear systems and linearised stability

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Linear systems and the linearisation principle]{.tag} Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix. The solution of $x' = Ax$ is $x(t) = e^{tA} x_0$.

1.  If every eigenvalue of $A$ has real part $< -\alpha < 0$, there is $C \ge 1$ such that $\|e^{tA}\| \le C e^{-\alpha t}$ for $t \ge 0$.
2.  In dimension 2, write $\tau = \mathrm{tr}\,A$ and $\Delta = \det A$. The origin is a saddle if $\Delta < 0$.

    If $\Delta > 0$, it is stable when $\tau < 0$ and unstable when $\tau > 0$; it is a focus when $\tau^2 < 4\Delta$ and a node otherwise.
3.  Let $x^*$ be an equilibrium of $x' = f(x)$ with $f$ of class $C^1$.

    If every eigenvalue of $Df(x^*)$ has negative real part, $x^*$ is locally exponentially stable. If one eigenvalue has positive real part, $x^*$ is unstable.

::: proof
*(1)* Put $A$ in Jordan form: each entry of $e^{tA}$ is a polynomial in $t$ times $e^{\lambda t}$, and $t^k e^{(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda + \alpha)t}$ is bounded.

*(2)* The eigenvalues are the roots of $\lambda^2 - \tau \lambda + \Delta = 0$. Their product is $\Delta$, their sum is $\tau$, and they are complex exactly when $\tau^2 < 4\Delta$.

*(3)* Write $x = x^* + y$, so that $y' = Ay + r(y)$ with $A = Df(x^*)$ and $\|r(y)\| \le \varepsilon \|y\|$ for $\|y\| \le \rho(\varepsilon)$. Variation of constants gives
$$
y(t) = e^{tA} y_0 + \int_0^t e^{(t-s)A}\, r(y(s))\, ds .
$$

With (1), the function $u(t) = e^{\alpha t}\|y(t)\|$ satisfies $u(t) \le C\|y_0\| + C\varepsilon \int_0^t u(s)\,ds$ as long as $y$ stays in the ball.

Grönwall's lemma gives $\|y(t)\| \le C \|y_0\| e^{-(\alpha - C\varepsilon)t}$, a decay as soon as $\varepsilon < \alpha / C$. A small enough $y_0$ never leaves the ball. The unstable case uses the same estimate backwards on the unstable subspace. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 0.3 Fourier modes of convolution operators

The neural fields of ch. 5 and the ring model of ch. 6 are built on convolution operators, and their linear stability always reduces to the following computation.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Convolutions are diagonal in Fourier modes]{.tag} Let $w \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ be even and $\hat w(k) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} w(x) e^{-ikx}\,dx$, a real number. For every $k \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}} w(x - y)\, e^{iky}\, dy = \hat w(k)\, e^{ikx}.
$$

On the circle $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ the same holds for $e^{ikx}$ with $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, with $\hat w_k = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} w(x) e^{-ikx}\,dx$.

::: proof
Substitute $z = x - y$: the integral becomes $e^{ikx} \int w(z) e^{-ikz}\,dz$. Evenness of $w$ makes the imaginary part $\int w(z) \sin(kz)\,dz$ vanish. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Example used throughout: the normalised Gaussian kernel and its transform,
$$
w(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}\,\sigma}\, e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}, \qquad \hat w(k) = e^{-\sigma^2 k^2/4}.
$$
::::

### 0.4 Probability toolkit

Chapters 4, 7 and 8 use Gaussian vectors, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, and the Poisson process. Two identities deserve a statement because they are the engine of the mean-field computations.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Gaussian integration by parts]{.tag} Let $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $f$ be $C^1$ with $f, f'$ of polynomial growth. Then (Stein's lemma)
$$
\mathbb{E}[Z f(Z)] = \mathbb{E}[f'(Z)].
$$

Let $(X_1, X_2)$ be a centred Gaussian pair with variances $q_1, q_2$ and covariance $c$, and $F, G$ smooth of polynomial growth. Then (Price's theorem)
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial c}\, \mathbb{E}[F(X_1) G(X_2)] = \mathbb{E}[F'(X_1)\, G'(X_2)].
$$

::: proof
Stein: integrate by parts, using $\varphi'(z) = -z \varphi(z)$ for the standard Gaussian density $\varphi$.

Price: the Gaussian density $p_c$ of $(X_1, X_2)$ satisfies $\partial_c p_c = \partial_{x_1}\partial_{x_2} p_c$. One checks it on the Fourier transform
$$
\hat p_c(\xi) = \exp\Big(-\tfrac12\big(q_1\xi_1^2 + 2c\,\xi_1\xi_2 + q_2\xi_2^2\big)\Big),
$$
whose $c$-derivative is $-\xi_1\xi_2$ times itself. Two integrations by parts move the derivatives onto $F$ and $G$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Inhomogeneous Poisson process]{.tag} A point process on $[0, \infty)$ with intensity $\lambda(t) \ge 0$ has independent counts on disjoint intervals, and the number of points in $[s, t]$ is Poisson with mean $\int_s^t \lambda$. In particular the probability of no point in $[s, t]$ is
$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{no point in } [s, t]) = \exp\Big(-\int_s^t \lambda(u)\, du\Big).
$$

Spike trains with a voltage-dependent intensity (ch. 8) and the input of a neuron from many independent cells (ch. 4) are modelled this way.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Vector fields that are Lipschitz on bounded sets, on $\mathbb{R}^n$ or on a Banach space, have unique maximal solutions; boundedness rules out blow-up.
-   Grönwall's lemma turns an integral inequality into an exponential bound; it drives every stability and convergence proof of the course.
-   An equilibrium is stable when the spectrum of the Jacobian lies in the open left half-plane; in the plane, trace and determinant decide.
-   Convolutions act diagonally on Fourier modes, with eigenvalue the Fourier transform of the kernel.
-   Gaussian integration by parts (Stein, Price) computes the averages that appear in mean-field equations.
:::

## 1. Neuron models {#ch1}

A neuron is a cell whose membrane potential can make a brief, stereotyped excursion, the action potential or spike, and pass it on to thousands of other cells. This chapter writes the models that reproduce this behaviour: the four equations of Hodgkin and Huxley, their two- and one-dimensional reductions, the synapses that connect neurons, and the cable equation that adds space.

### 1.1 The membrane as an electrical circuit

The lipid bilayer separating the inside of the cell from the outside behaves as a capacitor, with a specific capacitance of about 1 µF/cm². Ion pumps keep potassium concentrated inside the cell and sodium outside.

Ion channels are pores selective to one ion species. Each population of open channels acts as a conductance in series with a battery, whose voltage is the reversal potential of that ion.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Membrane equation and reversal potentials]{.tag} The membrane potential $V$ (inside minus outside) of an isopotential patch obeys
$$
C \frac{dV}{dt} = -\sum_{\text{ions}} g_{\text{ion}}\, (V - E_{\text{ion}}) + I_{\text{ext}},
$$
where $g_{\text{ion}} \ge 0$ is the conductance per unit area and $E_{\text{ion}}$ the reversal potential.

For an ion of valence $z$ with concentrations $c_{\text{in}}$ and $c_{\text{out}}$, $E_{\text{ion}}$ is the Nernst potential:
$$
E = \frac{RT}{zF} \ln \frac{c_{\text{out}}}{c_{\text{in}}}.
$$

It is the potential at which the Boltzmann factor $e^{-zFV/RT}$ balances the concentration ratio, so that no net flux crosses the open channels.
:::

At body temperature $RT/F \approx 26.7$ mV. With 140 mM of potassium inside and 5 mM outside, $E_K \approx -89$ mV; sodium, concentrated outside, has a positive reversal potential (Exercise 1).

### 1.2 The space-clamped Hodgkin–Huxley model

In 1952 Hodgkin and Huxley inserted a wire along the squid giant axon, which makes the potential uniform along the axon (the *space clamp*), and imposed $V$ by feedback (the *voltage clamp*). From the measured sodium and potassium currents they built the following model.

:::: def
[Definition 1.2 — The space-clamped Hodgkin–Huxley model]{.tag} With $V$ in mV, $t$ in ms and currents in µA/cm²:
$$
C \frac{dV}{dt} = I - \bar g_{Na}\, m^3 h\, (V - E_{Na}) - \bar g_K\, n^4 (V - E_K) - g_L (V - E_L),
$$
$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = \alpha_x(V)\,(1 - x) - \beta_x(V)\, x, \qquad x \in \{m, h, n\}.
$$

The squid parameters are $C = 1$ µF/cm² and the following conductances (mS/cm²) and reversal potentials (mV):
$$
\bar g_{Na} = 120, \quad \bar g_K = 36, \quad g_L = 0.3, \qquad E_{Na} = 50, \quad E_K = -77, \quad E_L = -54.4 .
$$

The rates, in ms⁻¹ and in the modern convention where rest is near $-65$ mV, are
$$
\alpha_n = \frac{0.01\,(V + 55)}{1 - e^{-(V+55)/10}}, \quad \beta_n = 0.125\, e^{-(V+65)/80},
$$
$$
\alpha_m = \frac{0.1\,(V + 40)}{1 - e^{-(V+40)/10}}, \quad \beta_m = 4\, e^{-(V+65)/18},
$$
$$
\alpha_h = 0.07\, e^{-(V+65)/20}, \quad \beta_h = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(V+35)/10}}.
$$

Equivalently $\dot x = (x_\infty(V) - x)/\tau_x(V)$, with
$$
x_\infty = \frac{\alpha_x}{\alpha_x + \beta_x}, \qquad \tau_x = \frac{1}{\alpha_x + \beta_x}.
$$
::::

The gating variables read as fractions of open gates. The variable $m$ activates the sodium current within a fraction of a millisecond; $h$ inactivates it, and $n$ activates the potassium current, both over several milliseconds.

The spike is a fast positive feedback followed by a slow negative one. A depolarisation opens sodium gates, the inward sodium current depolarises further, and $V$ shoots towards $E_{Na}$.

Then $h$ closes the sodium channels and $n$ opens the potassium channels, which bring $V$ back below rest. While $h$ and $n$ recover, a second spike is hard to trigger: this is the refractory period.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — An invariant box; global solutions]{.tag} Let $I \ge 0$, $V_- = E_K$ and $V_+ = \max(E_{Na},\, E_L + I/g_L)$. The box $[V_-, V_+] \times [0, 1]^3$ is forward-invariant for the Hodgkin–Huxley flow.

Consequently every solution starting in the box exists for all $t \ge 0$.

::: proof
The rates $\alpha_x, \beta_x$ are positive. On the face $x = 0$ the vector field gives $\dot x = \alpha_x > 0$, and on $x = 1$ it gives $\dot x = -\beta_x < 0$: the flow points inwards.

On the face $V = V_+$, both $V - E_{Na}$ and $V - E_K$ are non-negative, so the two active currents are outward and
$$
C \dot V \le I - g_L (V_+ - E_L) \le 0 .
$$

On $V = E_K$, the potassium term vanishes and the sodium and leak terms are inward, so $C \dot V \ge I \ge 0$.

The vector field is smooth (the apparent singularities of $\alpha_n, \alpha_m$ are removable), hence locally Lipschitz. Solutions stay in a compact set, so Theorem 0.1 excludes blow-up. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — The f–I curve of the Hodgkin–Huxley model]{.tag} We inject a constant current from rest and count spikes, defined as upward crossings of 0 mV, after a 100 ms transient.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

C, gNa, gK, gL = 1.0, 120.0, 36.0, 0.3          # uF/cm^2, mS/cm^2
ENa, EK, EL = 50.0, -77.0, -54.387              # mV

def rates(V):
    an = 0.01 * (V + 55) / (1 - np.exp(-(V + 55) / 10))
    bn = 0.125 * np.exp(-(V + 65) / 80)
    am = 0.1 * (V + 40) / (1 - np.exp(-(V + 40) / 10))
    bm = 4.0 * np.exp(-(V + 65) / 18)
    ah = 0.07 * np.exp(-(V + 65) / 20)
    bh = 1.0 / (1 + np.exp(-(V + 35) / 10))
    return an, bn, am, bm, ah, bh

def hh(t, y, I):
    V, n, m, h = y
    an, bn, am, bm, ah, bh = rates(V)
    dV = (I - gNa * m**3 * h * (V - ENa) - gK * n**4 * (V - EK) - gL * (V - EL)) / C
    return [dV, an * (1 - n) - bn * n, am * (1 - m) - bm * m, ah * (1 - h) - bh * h]

def rate_hz(I, T=300.0, y0=(-65.0, 0.317, 0.053, 0.596)):
    sol = solve_ivp(hh, (0, T), y0, args=(I,), max_step=0.1, rtol=1e-6)
    V, t = sol.y[0], sol.t
    up = np.where((V[:-1] < 0) & (V[1:] >= 0))[0]       # upward crossings of 0 mV
    late = t[up][t[up] > 100.0]                         # discard the transient
    return 0.0 if len(late) < 2 else 1000.0 / np.mean(np.diff(late))

for I in [0, 5, 6, 6.5, 7, 10, 20, 40]:
    print(f"I = {I:5.1f} uA/cm^2  ->  {rate_hz(I):6.1f} Hz")
```

Up to 6 µA/cm² the neuron returns to rest after at most one spike. At 6.5 µA/cm² it fires at 55 Hz, then at 58, 68, 87 and 109 Hz for 7, 10, 20 and 40 µA/cm².

The f–I curve jumps from 0 to about 55 Hz: the Hodgkin–Huxley neuron cannot fire slowly.

A linear stability computation of the resting state (Proposition 0.3) shows that rest stays stable up to $I \approx 9.8$ µA/cm². Between about 6.3 and 9.8, rest and repetitive firing coexist. Chapter 3 explains both facts by a subcritical Hopf bifurcation.
:::

### 1.3 Simplified models

Four variables are too many for a phase plane. Two observations reduce the model to two dimensions (Rinzel's reduction).

-   The sodium activation is much faster than the rest, so one may set $m = m_\infty(V)$.
-   Along trajectories, $h$ and $n$ are strongly anticorrelated. In the simulation of Example 1.4 at 10 µA/cm², $n + h$ stays between 0.78 and 0.85, and a linear fit, on samples equally spaced in time, gives $h \approx 0.87 - 1.07\, n$.

The result is a planar system in $(V, n)$ with a cubic-shaped $V$-nullcline. FitzHugh and, independently, Nagumo and coauthors kept only this geometry.

::: def
[Model — FitzHugh–Nagumo]{.tag} With a fast voltage-like variable $v$, a slow recovery variable $w$ and $0 < \varepsilon \ll 1$,
$$
\dot v = v - \frac{v^3}{3} - w + I, \qquad \dot w = \varepsilon\, (v + a - b\, w).
$$

FitzHugh's values are $a = 0.7$, $b = 0.8$ and $\varepsilon = 0.08$; the phase plane is analysed in ch. 2 and its bifurcations in ch. 3.
:::

The most drastic simplification keeps only the subthreshold dynamics and replaces the spike by a rule. This is the *integrate-and-fire* neuron, which goes back to Lapicque (1907).

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — Leaky integrate-and-fire: firing rate]{.tag} Let $\tau \dot V = -(V - E_L) + RI$ below a threshold $\theta$.

When $V$ reaches $\theta$, a spike is emitted, $V$ is reset to $V_r < \theta$ and held there during a refractory period $\tau_{\text{ref}}$.

For a constant current, write $V_\infty = E_L + RI$. If $V_\infty \le \theta$ the neuron never fires. Otherwise it fires periodically with period
$$
T = \tau_{\text{ref}} + \tau \ln \frac{V_\infty - V_r}{V_\infty - \theta}.
$$

::: proof
After the refractory period, the solution of the linear equation is
$$
V(t) = V_\infty + (V_r - V_\infty)\, e^{-t/\tau}.
$$

It increases to $V_\infty$. It reaches $\theta$ if and only if $V_\infty > \theta$, at the time obtained by solving $V(t) = \theta$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

As $V_\infty \downarrow \theta$, the rate $1/T$ tends to zero, but only logarithmically. The integrate-and-fire neuron can fire arbitrarily slowly, unlike Example 1.4.
::::

The quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron keeps the spike initiation as a smooth instability rather than a hard threshold. It is the normal form of the saddle-node bifurcation of ch. 3, and the building block of the neural mass of ch. 8.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.6 — Quadratic integrate-and-fire and the theta neuron]{.tag} Consider $\tau \dot V = V^2 + I$, where $V$ is reset from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$ at each spike.

1.  If $I < 0$, there are two equilibria $\pm\sqrt{-I}$: the negative one is the stable rest state, the positive one an unstable threshold.
2.  If $I > 0$, the neuron fires periodically with period $T = \pi\tau/\sqrt{I}$.
3.  The change of variables $V = \tan(\theta/2)$ turns the model into the theta neuron of Ermentrout and Kopell (1986), a smooth flow on the circle:
$$
\tau \dot\theta = (1 - \cos\theta) + (1 + \cos\theta)\, I .
$$

::: proof
*(1)* The equilibria solve $V^2 = -I$, and the derivative $2V/\tau$ of the right-hand side is negative at $-\sqrt{-I}$ and positive at $+\sqrt{-I}$.

*(2)* The time to go from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ is
$$
T = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{\tau\, dV}{V^2 + I} = \frac{\tau \pi}{\sqrt{I}}.
$$

*(3)* We have $\dot V = \tfrac12 (1 + V^2)\, \dot\theta$ and $1 + V^2 = 1/\cos^2(\theta/2)$. Hence
$$
\tau\dot\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2) + 2I\cos^2(\theta/2),
$$
and the half-angle formulas conclude. The spike $V = +\infty$ is the point $\theta = \pi$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The firing frequency $\sqrt{I}/(\pi\tau)$ starts from zero with a square-root law. This is the signature of the first excitability class (class 1) discussed in ch. 3.5.
::::

Izhikevich's model (2003) adds a slow adaptation variable to a quadratic neuron. With four parameters it reproduces most firing patterns recorded in cortex (regular spiking, bursting, fast spiking), at the cost of one reset rule.

### 1.4 Synapse models

At a chemical synapse, a presynaptic spike releases neurotransmitter, which opens receptor channels on the postsynaptic membrane. The postsynaptic neuron sees a transient conductance.

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Synaptic currents]{.tag} The synaptic current is
$$
I_{\text{syn}}(t) = \bar g_{\text{syn}}\, s(t)\, (V - E_{\text{syn}}),
$$
where $s \in [0, 1]$ is the fraction of open receptor channels. Three standard choices for $s$:

1.  *Kinetic model* (Destexhe, Mainen and Sejnowski, 1994): $\dot s = \alpha\, T(t)\, (1 - s) - \beta s$, where $T(t)$ is the transmitter concentration, a pulse of about 1 ms after each presynaptic spike.
2.  *Alpha function*: $s(t) = \sum_k \alpha(t - t_k)$, with spike times $t_k$ and $\alpha(t) = (t/\tau_s)\, e^{1 - t/\tau_s}$ for $t \ge 0$.
3.  *Exponential synapse*: $\tau_s \dot s = -s + \tau_s \sum_k \delta(t - t_k)$, that is a jump of $1$ at each spike followed by an exponential decay. Here $s$ counts recent spikes and can exceed $1$; it is then rescaled into the conductance $\bar g_{\text{syn}}$.

The reversal potential decides the sign. For glutamate (AMPA and NMDA receptors) $E_{\text{syn}}$ is near 0 mV, and the synapse is excitatory. For GABA$_A$ receptors it is near $-70$ mV, and the synapse is inhibitory.

In the *current-based* approximation, $V - E_{\text{syn}}$ is frozen to a constant, and the input becomes a filtered spike train $J \sum_k \varepsilon(t - t_k)$.
:::

The exponential synapse is a linear filter. If the presynaptic train is Poisson with rate $\nu$, Campbell's theorem gives the mean and variance of $s$ in the stationary regime:
$$
\mathbb{E}[s] = \nu \tau_s, \qquad \mathrm{Var}[s] = \frac{\nu \tau_s}{2}.
$$

These two numbers are the drift and the noise of the diffusion approximation of ch. 4.5.

### 1.5 Spatial models: the cable equation

Dendrites and axons are thin cylinders, and the potential varies along them. Charge conservation in a cylinder of radius $a$, with axial resistivity $r_L$ and membrane capacitance $c_m$ per unit area, gives the cable equation
$$
c_m \frac{\partial V}{\partial t} = \frac{a}{2 r_L} \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial x^2} - i_{\text{ion}} + i_{\text{ext}}.
$$

For a passive membrane, $i_{\text{ion}} = (V - E_L)/r_m$, where $r_m$ is the specific membrane resistance. With $u = V - E_L$ it reads
$$
\tau_m \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \lambda^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - u + r_m\, i_{\text{ext}}, \qquad \tau_m = r_m c_m, \quad \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{a\, r_m}{2 r_L}} .
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — The passive cable]{.tag}

1.  On a semi-infinite cable held at $u(0) = u_0$, the steady state decays over the length constant: $u(x) = u_0\, e^{-x/\lambda}$.
2.  On an infinite cable, the response to a unit charge injected at $x = 0$, $t = 0$ is the Green's function
$$
G(x, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi D t}}\, \exp\Big(-\frac{x^2}{4 D t} - \frac{t}{\tau_m}\Big), \qquad D = \frac{\lambda^2}{\tau_m}.
$$
3.  With active Hodgkin–Huxley currents, the conduction velocity of a propagated spike scales like $\sqrt{a}$.

::: proof
*(1)* The steady state solves $\lambda^2 u'' = u$; the solution bounded at infinity is $u_0 e^{-x/\lambda}$.

*(2)* Write $u = e^{-t/\tau_m} K$. Then $K$ solves the heat equation $\partial_t K = D\, \partial_{xx} K$ with $K(\cdot, 0) = \delta_0$, whose solution is the Gaussian kernel.

*(3)* The ionic currents are per unit area, so in the variables $x/\lambda$ and $t/\tau_m$ the active cable equation no longer involves $a$. A travelling pulse of dimensionless speed $c_0$ has physical speed $c_0 \lambda / \tau_m$, which is proportional to $\sqrt{a}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Hodgkin and Huxley solved the active cable equation numerically and obtained a conduction velocity close to the measured one. In practice, a dendritic tree is cut into short compartments coupled by axial conductances, each one a copy of Definition 1.1: these compartmental models are what simulators such as NEURON integrate.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   The membrane is a capacitor in parallel with ionic conductances, each with its own reversal potential given by the Nernst formula.
-   The Hodgkin–Huxley model couples the voltage to three gating variables; fast sodium activation and slow recovery produce the spike.
-   Its f–I curve jumps from zero to about 55 Hz, and rest coexists with firing over a range of currents.
-   Reductions keep the geometry (FitzHugh–Nagumo) or the timing (integrate-and-fire, quadratic integrate-and-fire with period πτ/√I).
-   Synapses are transient conductances, often modelled as linear filters of spike trains.
-   The passive cable has a length constant λ and a Gaussian Green's function; active cables carry pulses whose speed grows like √a.
:::

## 2. Dynamical systems {#ch2}

The models of ch. 1 are too nonlinear to solve in closed form, but their qualitative behaviour can be read from the geometry of their solutions. This chapter gives the vocabulary of that geometry: orbits and phase portraits, invariant manifolds, the equivalence of two systems, structural stability and the centre manifold, the tool that reduces a high-dimensional system to the few directions where something happens.

### 2.1 Flows, orbits and phase portraits

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Flow, orbit, invariant set, limit set]{.tag} Let $f$ be of class $C^1$ on an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^n$.

Write $\varphi_t(x_0)$ for the solution of $\dot x = f(x)$ at time $t$ starting from $x_0$; the family $(\varphi_t)$ is the *flow*.

-   The *orbit* of $x_0$ is the curve $\{\varphi_t(x_0)\}$, over the times where it is defined.
-   A set $S$ is *invariant* if $\varphi_t(S) \subset S$ for all $t$, and *forward-invariant* (or trapping) if this holds for $t \ge 0$.
-   The $\omega$-*limit set* $\omega(x_0)$ is the set of points $y$ such that $\varphi_{t_k}(x_0) \to y$ along some sequence $t_k \to +\infty$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Equilibria, cycles and phase portrait]{.tag} An *equilibrium* is a zero of $f$. A *periodic orbit* is a closed orbit that is not an equilibrium; a *limit cycle* is an isolated periodic orbit. The *phase portrait* is the partition of $U$ into orbits, drawn with its equilibria, cycles and separatrices.

In the plane, the *nullclines* are the curves $\{f_1 = 0\}$ and $\{f_2 = 0\}$. Equilibria lie at their intersections, and the direction of the flow is constant in each region they delimit.
:::

In the plane, the topology of the plane severely limits what orbits can do.

::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Poincaré–Bendixson]{.tag} Let $n = 2$ and suppose the forward orbit of $x_0$ stays in a compact set $K \subset U$ that contains no equilibrium. Then $\omega(x_0)$ is a periodic orbit.

In particular, a compact trapping region without equilibria contains a periodic orbit.

*Proof*: see Perko (2001, §3.7). The key step: a segment transverse to the flow is crossed by the orbit at points that are monotone along the segment, because of the Jordan curve theorem; hence $\omega(x_0)$ meets the segment at most once, and this forces it to be a closed orbit.
:::

:::: ex
[Example 2.4 — The phase plane of FitzHugh–Nagumo]{.tag} Take $a = 0.7$, $b = 0.8$, $\varepsilon = 0.08$.

*Equilibrium.* The nullclines are the cubic $w = v - v^3/3 + I$ and the line $w = (v + a)/b$. The equilibrium abscissa $v^*$ solves
$$
v - \frac{v^3}{3} - \frac{v + a}{b} + I = 0 .
$$
The left-hand side has derivative $1 - v^2 - 1/b < 0$ since $b < 1$, so there is exactly one equilibrium for every $I$.

*Linearisation.* The Jacobian at the equilibrium and its two invariants are
$$
J = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - v^{*2} & -1 \\ \varepsilon & -\varepsilon b \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathrm{tr}\, J = 1 - v^{*2} - \varepsilon b, \qquad \det J = \varepsilon\,\big(1 - b(1 - v^{*2})\big).
$$

Here $\det J > 0$ whenever $\mathrm{tr}\,J \ge 0$, so by Proposition 0.3 the equilibrium is unstable exactly when $v^{*2} < 1 - \varepsilon b$. This happens for $I$ between two values $I_1$ and $I_2$, computed below.

*A trapping region.* Let $L = \varepsilon v^2/2 + w^2/2$. The cross terms cancel and
$$
\dot L = \varepsilon \Big( v^2 - \frac{v^4}{3} + I v + a w - b w^2 \Big),
$$
which is negative outside a large disc. So large sublevel sets of $L$ are trapping regions.

For $I_1 < I < I_2$, remove a small neighbourhood of the repelling equilibrium. The annulus that remains is trapping and contains no equilibrium, so Theorem 2.3 gives a periodic orbit: the neuron fires repetitively.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

a, b, eps = 0.7, 0.8, 0.08                        # FitzHugh's classical values

def equilibrium(I):
    # v - v^3/3 - (v + a)/b + I = 0 has a single root since b < 1
    v = brentq(lambda v: v - v**3 / 3 - (v + a) / b + I, -3, 3)
    return v, (v + a) / b

def jacobian(v):
    return np.array([[1 - v**2, -1.0], [eps, -eps * b]])

for I in [0.0, 0.3, 0.33, 0.34, 0.5, 1.0, 1.4, 1.5]:
    v, w = equilibrium(I)
    J = jacobian(v)
    tr, det = np.trace(J), np.linalg.det(J)
    kind = ("focus" if tr**2 < 4 * det else "node") if det > 0 else "saddle"
    print(f"I={I:4.2f}  v*={v:+.4f}  tr={tr:+.4f}  det={det:.4f}  "
          f"{'unstable' if tr > 0 else 'stable'} {kind}")

# Hopf points: tr J = 0  <=>  v*^2 = 1 - eps*b
vH = np.sqrt(1 - eps * b)
for v in (-vH, vH):
    print(f"Hopf at v*={v:+.4f}, I_H={(v + a) / b - v + v**3 / 3:.4f}, "
          f"omega={np.sqrt(np.linalg.det(jacobian(v))):.4f}")
```

At $I = 0$ the equilibrium is $v^* = -1.1994$, a stable focus with eigenvalues $-0.251 \pm 0.212\,i$. The trace vanishes at
$$
I_1 \approx 0.3313, \qquad I_2 \approx 1.4187,
$$
with $\sqrt{\det J} \approx 0.2755$ at both points. Between them, the equilibrium is an unstable focus or node.
::::

### 2.2 Invariant manifolds

An equilibrium $x^*$ is *hyperbolic* if no eigenvalue of $A = Df(x^*)$ lies on the imaginary axis. The generalised eigenspaces for eigenvalues of negative and positive real part are the stable and unstable subspaces $E^s$ and $E^u$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — Stable and unstable manifolds]{.tag} Let $f$ be of class $C^k$, $k \ge 1$, and $x^*$ a hyperbolic equilibrium. The sets
$$
W^s(x^*) = \{x : \varphi_t(x) \to x^* \text{ as } t \to +\infty\}, \qquad W^u(x^*) = \{x : \varphi_t(x) \to x^* \text{ as } t \to -\infty\}
$$
are invariant.

Near $x^*$ they are embedded $C^k$ manifolds, of dimensions $\dim E^s$ and $\dim E^u$. At $x^*$ they are tangent to the stable and unstable subspaces respectively.

*Proof sketch* (Lyapunov–Perron): a point lies on the local stable manifold if and only if its solution stays bounded for $t \ge 0$. Bounded solutions are fixed points of an integral equation that integrates the unstable component backwards from $+\infty$; for initial data close to $x^*$, this equation is a contraction (Guckenheimer and Holmes, 1983, §1.3; Kuznetsov, 2004, §2.2).

*Illustration.* For $\dot x = x$, $\dot y = -y + x^2$, the origin is a saddle. The stable manifold is the axis $\{x = 0\}$. The unstable manifold is the parabola $y = x^2/3$: along it,
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\Big(\frac{x^2}{3}\Big) = \frac{2x^2}{3} = -\frac{x^2}{3} + x^2 ,
$$
which is exactly $\dot y$, so the parabola is invariant, and it is tangent to $E^u$ = the $x$-axis.
::::

Invariant manifolds are the thresholds of neuroscience. In a model where rest coexists with a saddle (the Morris–Lecar model in its first-class regime, ch. 3.5), the stable manifold of the saddle separates the initial conditions that return to rest from those that produce a spike: it is a true, sharp threshold.

FitzHugh–Nagumo has no saddle at small $I$, and its threshold is only a narrow region of rapid change. FitzHugh called it a quasi-threshold: responses grow steeply but continuously with the stimulus.

### 2.3 Equivalence and the topological classification of equilibria

When are two dynamical systems "the same"? Requiring identical solutions is too strict; the right notion keeps the orbits and forgets the parametrisation.

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Topological equivalence and conjugacy]{.tag} Consider two flows, $\varphi$ on $U$ and $\psi$ on $V$.

They are *topologically equivalent* if there is a homeomorphism $h : U \to V$ that maps orbits of $\varphi$ onto orbits of $\psi$ and preserves the direction of time.

They are *topologically conjugate* if moreover $h$ preserves time itself:
$$
h \circ \varphi_t = \psi_t \circ h \quad \text{for all } t .
$$

*Local* versions near two points replace $U$ and $V$ by neighbourhoods. When $h$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, the equivalence is *smooth*.
:::

Smooth conjugacy is too fine for classification: it preserves the eigenvalues of the linearisation, which vary continuously. Topological equivalence forgets them and keeps only signs.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — Hartman–Grobman]{.tag} If $x^*$ is a hyperbolic equilibrium of $\dot x = f(x)$, the flow near $x^*$ is topologically conjugate to the linear flow $e^{tA}$ near $0$, where $A = Df(x^*)$.

*Proof*: see Perko (2001, §2.8). The key step: for the time-one maps $T = e^A + \phi$, with $\phi$ small and Lipschitz, the conjugacy $h = I + \eta$ solves a fixed-point equation for $\eta$ in the space of bounded continuous maps.

Split along $E^s$ and $E^u$, this equation is a contraction, because $e^A$ contracts $E^s$ and expands $E^u$.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.8 — Topological classification of hyperbolic equilibria]{.tag} Let $A$ and $B$ be hyperbolic $n \times n$ matrices with $n_s(A)$ and $n_s(B)$ eigenvalues of negative real part.

The flows $e^{tA}$ and $e^{tB}$ are topologically conjugate if and only if
$$
n_s(A) = n_s(B).
$$

Consequently a hyperbolic equilibrium is locally topologically equivalent to the standard saddle $\dot x_s = -x_s$, $\dot x_u = x_u$, with $x_s \in \mathbb{R}^{n_s}$ and $x_u \in \mathbb{R}^{n - n_s}$.

::: proof
*Sufficiency, stable case* ($n_s = n$). There is a positive definite quadratic form $Q$ with $\frac{d}{dt}Q(e^{tA}x) < 0$ for $x \ne 0$, for instance $Q(x) = \int_0^\infty |e^{sA}x|^2\, ds$.

Hence every non-zero orbit crosses the ellipsoid $\{Q = 1\}$ exactly once. Write $x = e^{tA}\xi$ with $Q(\xi) = 1$, and set
$$
h(x) = e^{-t}\, \frac{\xi}{|\xi|}, \qquad h(0) = 0 .
$$
Then $h$ is a homeomorphism that conjugates $e^{tA}$ to $e^{-t}\,\mathrm{Id}$.

*General case.* Apply this separately on $E^s$ and, reversing time, on $E^u$, and take the product.

*Necessity.* The stable set $\{x : e^{tA}x \to 0\}$ is the subspace $E^s$, and a conjugacy maps it homeomorphically onto $E^s(B)$. Invariance of domain forbids homeomorphisms between Euclidean spaces of different dimensions. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In the plane there are therefore only three topological types of hyperbolic equilibria: sink, source and saddle. A stable node and a stable focus are topologically equivalent; the spiralling, visible as damped oscillations of the membrane potential, is a smooth invariant, not a topological one.

### 2.4 Structural stability

A model is useful only if its qualitative predictions survive small errors in its equations. Structural stability makes this precise.

::: def
[Definition 2.9 — Structural stability]{.tag} Let $D$ be a compact region with smooth boundary, crossed inwards by the flow of $f$. The system $\dot x = f(x)$ is *structurally stable* on $D$ if there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every $g$ with
$$
\|f - g\|_{C^1(D)} < \varepsilon
$$
defines a flow topologically equivalent to that of $f$ on $D$.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.10 — Andronov–Pontryagin]{.tag} A smooth planar system on a disc whose boundary is crossed inwards is structurally stable if and only if:

1.  it has finitely many equilibria and periodic orbits, all hyperbolic (for a cycle: the multiplier of its Poincaré return map is not $1$);
2.  no orbit connects two saddles.

Peixoto (1962) extended the result to compact orientable surfaces and showed that structurally stable systems form an open and dense set there. In dimension three and more, density fails (Smale).

*Proof*: see Kuznetsov (2004, §2.5) and the references there.
:::

The centre $\dot x = -y$, $\dot y = x$ is not structurally stable. The perturbation $\dot x = \varepsilon x - y$, $\dot y = x + \varepsilon y$ turns it into a focus, stable or unstable according to the sign of $\varepsilon$.

In a generic one-parameter family of planar models, structurally unstable systems occur at isolated parameter values. These are the bifurcation points of ch. 3, where the conclusions of a model change.

### 2.5 The centre manifold in finite dimension

At a non-hyperbolic equilibrium the linearisation does not decide stability, and something happens on the eigenvalues of zero real part. The centre manifold isolates these directions.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.11 — Centre manifold theorem and reduction principle]{.tag} Let $\dot x = Ax + F(x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $F$ is of class $C^k$ with $k \ge 2$ and vanishes at the origin together with its derivative.

Split $\mathbb{R}^n = E^c \oplus E^s \oplus E^u$ according to eigenvalues of zero, negative and positive real part.

1.  There is a locally invariant $C^k$ manifold $W^c$, the graph of a map $h : E^c \to E^s \oplus E^u$ with $h(0) = 0$ and $Dh(0) = 0$.
2.  (Pliss, Shoshitaishvili) Near $0$, the system is topologically equivalent to the decoupled system
$$
\dot u = A_c u + P_c F\big(u + h(u)\big), \qquad \dot y_s = -y_s, \qquad \dot y_u = y_u ,
$$
with $u \in E^c$. In particular, when $E^u = \{0\}$, the origin is stable if and only if it is stable for the reduced equation in $u$.

The manifold need not be unique, nor $C^\infty$ for a $C^\infty$ field, but its Taylor expansion at $0$ is unique.

*Proof sketch*: multiply $F$ by a cut-off so that it becomes globally Lipschitz with a small constant. $W^c$ is then the set of initial conditions whose solutions grow at most like $e^{\eta |t|}$ for a small $\eta$. These solutions are the fixed points of an integral equation that is a contraction in a weighted space of continuous functions (Carr, 1981; Haragus and Iooss, 2011).
::::

To compute $h$, write that the graph is invariant. With $E^h = E^s \oplus E^u$ and the projections $P_c, P_h$:
$$
Dh(u)\,\big[A_c u + P_c F(u + h(u))\big] = A_h\, h(u) + P_h F\big(u + h(u)\big).
$$

This equation is solved order by order in the Taylor expansion of $h$.

:::: ex
[Example 2.12 — A centre manifold by hand]{.tag} Consider
$$
\dot x = x y, \qquad \dot y = -y - x^2 .
$$

The linearisation has eigenvalues $0$ and $-1$, so it decides nothing. Look for $y = h(x) = \alpha x^2 + \beta x^3 + \gamma x^4 + O(x^5)$.

-   The invariance equation reads $h'(x)\, x\, h(x) = -h(x) - x^2$.
-   Its left-hand side is $2\alpha^2 x^4 + O(x^5)$.
-   Matching $x^2$, $x^3$ and $x^4$ gives $\alpha = -1$, $\beta = 0$ and $\gamma = -2\alpha^2 = -2$.

The centre manifold and the reduced equation are
$$
h(x) = -x^2 - 2x^4 + O(x^5), \qquad \dot x = x\, h(x) = -x^3 + O(x^5).
$$

By Theorem 2.11 the origin is asymptotically stable, with a slow algebraic decay $x(t) \sim 1/\sqrt{2t}$, invisible to the linearisation.

Setting $\dot y = 0$ ("adiabatic elimination") would give $y = -x^2$: the correct first term, but not the next one.
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Orbits, invariant sets and limit sets describe the qualitative behaviour; in the plane, Poincaré–Bendixson turns a trapping region without equilibria into a cycle.
-   FitzHugh–Nagumo has one equilibrium, unstable for 0.3313 < I < 1.4187, where a periodic orbit exists.
-   Hyperbolic equilibria have smooth stable and unstable manifolds; the stable manifold of a saddle is a sharp firing threshold.
-   Hartman–Grobman and Theorem 2.8: near a hyperbolic equilibrium only the number of stable eigenvalues matters; node and focus are topologically equivalent.
-   Andronov–Pontryagin: planar systems are structurally stable when everything is hyperbolic and no saddle connection exists; failures are bifurcations.
-   The centre manifold carries the dynamics of the non-hyperbolic directions; it is computed from the invariance equation, order by order.
:::

## 3. Bifurcation theory {#ch3}

When a parameter of a model (an injected current, a coupling strength) crosses a critical value, the phase portrait can change: equilibria appear or disappear, lose stability, give birth to oscillations. This chapter classifies the generic ways this happens, reduces each to a normal form, and uses them to explain the excitability of neurons and, through symmetry, the patterns of ch. 6.

### 3.1 What is a bifurcation?

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Bifurcation, codimension]{.tag} Consider a family $\dot x = f(x, \mu)$ with $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^p$. A value $\mu_0$ is a *bifurcation value* if there are parameter values arbitrarily close to $\mu_0$ whose phase portraits are not topologically equivalent to the one at $\mu_0$.

The *codimension* of a bifurcation is the number of independent equality conditions that define it. A generic one-parameter family meets only codimension-one bifurcations.
:::

A local bifurcation of an equilibrium requires a non-hyperbolic equilibrium. Indeed, if $D_x f(x_0, \mu_0)$ is invertible, the implicit function theorem continues the equilibrium as a smooth curve $x^*(\mu)$. Its eigenvalues move continuously, so the number of stable ones does not change, and Theorem 2.8 gives local equivalence.

For equilibria, the two codimension-one cases are therefore a zero eigenvalue (saddle-node) and a pair of purely imaginary eigenvalues (Hopf). Symmetry (ch. 3.6) or a trivial solution that persists for all parameters changes the generic picture.

### 3.2 One-dimensional bifurcations

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Saddle-node (fold) bifurcation]{.tag} Let $\dot x = f(x, \mu)$ with $x, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$, $f$ smooth, and at $(0, 0)$:
$$
f = 0, \qquad f_x = 0, \qquad f_{xx} \ne 0, \qquad f_\mu \ne 0 .
$$

Near $(0, 0)$ the equilibria form a curve $\mu = m(x)$ with $m(0) = m'(0) = 0$ and $m''(0) = -f_{xx}/f_\mu$. There are two equilibria, one stable and one unstable, on one side of $\mu = 0$, and none on the other.

The family is locally topologically equivalent to the normal form
$$
\dot x = \beta \pm x^2 .
$$

::: proof
Since $f_\mu \ne 0$, the implicit function theorem solves $f(x, \mu) = 0$ as $\mu = m(x)$.

Differentiating $f(x, m(x)) = 0$ once gives $f_x + f_\mu m' = 0$, hence $m'(0) = 0$. Differentiating twice gives $f_{xx} + f_\mu m''(0) = 0$ at the origin.

So $m$ has a strict extremum at $0$: each $\mu$ on one side of $0$ has exactly two preimages $x_- < 0 < x_+$, and the other side none.

On the curve, $f_x(x, m(x)) = -f_\mu\, m'(x) = f_{xx}\, x + O(x^2)$, which has opposite signs at $x_-$ and $x_+$: one equilibrium is stable, the other unstable.

Two scalar flows with the same ordered list of equilibria and the same stabilities are topologically equivalent: map equilibria to equilibria and the intervals between them monotonically onto each other. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Transcritical and pitchfork bifurcations]{.tag} Suppose $f(0, \mu) = 0$ for all $\mu$, $f_x(0, 0) = 0$ and $f_{x\mu}(0, 0) \ne 0$.

1.  If $f_{xx}(0, 0) \ne 0$, a second branch of equilibria crosses $x = 0$ transversally and the two branches exchange stability (transcritical). Normal form: $\dot x = \beta x - x^2$.
2.  If $f$ is odd in $x$ (a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry $x \mapsto -x$) and $f_{xxx}(0, 0) \ne 0$, a pair of symmetric equilibria $\pm x(\mu)$ appears on one side (pitchfork).

    Normal form: $\dot x = \beta x \mp x^3$, supercritical with the minus sign, subcritical with the plus sign.

::: proof
Write $f(x, \mu) = x\, g(x, \mu)$, with $g(0, 0) = f_x(0, 0) = 0$ and $g_\mu(0, 0) = f_{x\mu}(0, 0) \ne 0$. The non-trivial equilibria solve $g = 0$, that is $\mu = m(x)$ by the implicit function theorem.

In case 1, $m'(0) = -g_x/g_\mu = -f_{xx}/(2 f_{x\mu}) \ne 0$: a line crossing the trivial branch.

In case 2, $g$ is even in $x$, so $m$ is even with $m''(0) \ne 0$ given by $f_{xxx}$: a parabola.

The stabilities follow from the sign of $f_x$ along each branch, as in Theorem 3.2. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — Bistability and hysteresis in a rate model]{.tag} A population with recurrent excitation is described by its rate $r$:
$$
\tau \dot r = -r + S(w r + I), \qquad S(u) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-u}} .
$$

*Equilibria.* Parametrise them by the total input $u = wr + I$: they satisfy $r = S(u)$ and $I = u - w S(u)$.

*Folds.* A fold occurs where $w S'(u) = 1$. Since $S' = S(1 - S) \le 1/4$, folds exist if and only if $w > 4$. For $w = 6$, they sit at $S = (1 \pm 1/\sqrt{3})/2$, that is $u = \pm 1.3170$, and the fold currents are
$$
I_- = -3.4151, \qquad I_+ = -2.5849 .
$$

Theorem 3.2 applies there: $f_{rr} = w^2 S''(u) \ne 0$ because $S \ne 1/2$ at the folds, and $f_I = S'(u) \ne 0$.

*Hysteresis.* For $I_- < I < I_+$, a low-activity and a high-activity state coexist with an unstable state between them. Raising $I$ past $I_+$ makes the rate jump up; it falls back only when $I$ goes below $I_-$. Such bistable populations are a classical model of persistent activity in working memory.
:::

### 3.3 The Hopf bifurcation

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.5 — Andronov–Hopf bifurcation]{.tag} Let $\dot x = f(x, \mu)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with an equilibrium at $0$ for all $\mu$ and eigenvalues $\alpha(\mu) \pm i\omega(\mu)$, where
$$
\alpha(0) = 0, \qquad \omega(0) = \omega_0 > 0, \qquad \alpha'(0) \ne 0 .
$$

Then there are complex coordinates in which the system reads
$$
\dot z = (\alpha(\mu) + i\omega(\mu))\, z + c_1(\mu)\, |z|^2 z + O(|z|^4).
$$

Let $\ell_1 = \mathrm{Re}\, c_1(0)/\omega_0$ be the *first Lyapunov coefficient*. If $\ell_1 \ne 0$, then for small $\mu$:

1.  If $\ell_1 < 0$ (supercritical), a unique stable limit cycle exists on the side $\alpha(\mu) > 0$, of radius $\sqrt{-\alpha/\mathrm{Re}\,c_1}\,(1 + o(1))$.
2.  If $\ell_1 > 0$ (subcritical), a unique unstable limit cycle exists on the side $\alpha(\mu) < 0$. When $\alpha$ crosses $0$, solutions leave the neighbourhood: the system jumps to a distant attractor.

In both cases the period of the cycle tends to $2\pi/\omega_0$.

::: proof
*Normal form.* The change of variables of Theorem 3.7 below (§3.4) removes all quadratic terms and all cubic terms except $|z|^2 z$.

*Polar coordinates.* With $z = \rho e^{i\vartheta}$,
$$
\dot \rho = \rho\, \big(\alpha + \mathrm{Re}\,c_1\, \rho^2\big) + O(\rho^4), \qquad \dot\vartheta = \omega + O(\rho^2).
$$

*Return map.* On the half-line $\vartheta = 0$, the return map satisfies, up to higher-order terms in $\alpha$,
$$
P(\rho) - \rho = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}\, \rho\,\big(\alpha + \mathrm{Re}\,c_1\, \rho^2\big) + O(\rho^4).
$$

A cycle is a fixed point $\rho > 0$. Divide by $\rho$ and apply the implicit function theorem in the variable $\rho^2$: the solution exists exactly when $\alpha$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,c_1$ have opposite signs, and it has the stated size.

The sign of $P'(\rho) - 1$ there is the sign of $-\alpha$, which gives the stability. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a planar system already written with linear part $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\omega \\ \omega & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and nonlinear terms $f, g$, the classical formula of Guckenheimer and Holmes (1983, §3.4) gives $\mathrm{Re}\,c_1 = a$ with
$$
16 a = f_{xxx} + f_{xyy} + g_{xxy} + g_{yyy} + \frac{1}{\omega}\big[f_{xy}(f_{xx} + f_{yy}) - g_{xy}(g_{xx} + g_{yy}) - f_{xx} g_{xx} + f_{yy} g_{yy}\big].
$$

Kuznetsov (2004, §3.5) gives a coordinate-free formula with the right and left eigenvectors of the Jacobian. Written with the bilinear and trilinear forms of the vector field, it holds in any dimension (same book, ch. 5). It is the one used below.

:::: ex
[Example 3.6 — FitzHugh–Nagumo: a subcritical Hopf bifurcation]{.tag} At the first Hopf point of Example 2.4, $v^* = -\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon b}$ and $I_1 \approx 0.3313$.

Shifting the equilibrium to $0$, the nonlinear part of the $v$-equation is $-v^* x^2 - x^3/3$: it defines the bilinear and trilinear forms $B$ and $C$ below.

```python
import numpy as np
a, b, eps = 0.7, 0.8, 0.08
vH = -np.sqrt(1 - eps * b)                        # lower Hopf point
A = np.array([[1 - vH**2, -1.0], [eps, -eps * b]])
B = lambda x, y: np.array([-2 * vH * x[0] * y[0], 0.0])   # quadratic part at the equilibrium
C = lambda x, y, z: np.array([-2 * x[0] * y[0] * z[0], 0.0])

lam, Q = np.linalg.eig(A)
k = np.argmax(lam.imag); om = lam[k].imag; q = Q[:, k]
lamT, P = np.linalg.eig(A.T)
p = P[:, np.argmin(np.abs(lamT + 1j * om))]       # A^T p = -i om p
p = p / np.conj(np.vdot(p, q))                    # normalise <p, q> = 1 (<x,y> = conj(x).y)
dot = lambda u, v: np.vdot(u, v)
l1 = np.real(dot(p, C(q, q, q.conj()))
             - 2 * dot(p, B(q, np.linalg.solve(A, B(q, q.conj()))))
             + dot(p, B(q.conj(), np.linalg.solve(2j * om * np.eye(2) - A, B(q, q))))) / (2 * om)
print(f"omega = {om:.4f}, first Lyapunov coefficient l1 = {l1:.4f}")
```

The output is $\omega_0 = 0.2755$ and
$$
\ell_1 \approx 0.97 > 0 :
$$
the bifurcation is subcritical.

The value $0.97$ uses Kuznetsov's normalisation $\langle q, q\rangle = \langle p, q\rangle = 1$; rescaling the coordinates changes the magnitude of $\ell_1$, never its sign.

A simulation confirms the picture. At $I = 0.33$, just below $I_1$, the stable focus coexists with a large relaxation cycle; at $I = 0.32$ the large cycle no longer exists. Just above $I_1$, the neuron jumps to that cycle, of period about 48 time units: the oscillation starts with a finite frequency and a large amplitude.

The Hodgkin–Huxley model behaves the same way. Rinzel and Miller (1980) computed its subcritical Hopf point near $I \approx 9.8$ µA/cm² and the fold of cycles near $6.3$ µA/cm² that ends the bistable range seen in Example 1.4.
::::

### 3.4 Centre manifold reduction and normal forms

A bifurcation of an equilibrium in $\mathbb{R}^n$ involves only the eigenvalues on the imaginary axis. The parameter-dependent centre manifold makes this exact.

Append $\dot\mu = 0$ to the system. The parameters become centre directions, and Theorem 2.11 gives a manifold of dimension $\dim E^c + p$ that contains every small bounded solution for every small $\mu$.

For the Hopf bifurcation of the four-dimensional Hodgkin–Huxley model, the reduced system is two-dimensional, and Theorem 3.5 applies to it. For a fold, it is one-dimensional, and Theorem 3.2 applies.

On the centre manifold, polynomial changes of variables simplify the equations further.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.7 — Poincaré normal form]{.tag} Let $\dot x = Ax + F_2(x) + F_3(x) + \dots$, with $F_k$ homogeneous of degree $k$ and $A = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$ (possibly complex).

A monomial $x^m e_i$, with $m \in \mathbb{N}^n$ and $|m| = k$, is *resonant* if
$$
\lambda_i = \sum_j m_j \lambda_j .
$$

For each $k \ge 2$, a change of variables $x = y + h_k(y)$, with $h_k$ homogeneous of degree $k$, removes all non-resonant monomials of degree $k$ without changing the lower-order terms.

::: proof
Substituting $x = y + h_k(y)$ and keeping the terms of degree $k$ gives
$$
\dot y = Ay + F_2 + \dots + F_{k-1} + \big[F_k - L_A h_k\big] + O(|y|^{k+1}),
$$
where $L_A h := Dh(y)\, A y - A h(y)$ is the homological operator.

On a monomial, $L_A(y^m e_i) = (m \cdot \lambda - \lambda_i)\, y^m e_i$. So $L_A$ is diagonal on monomials, invertible on the non-resonant ones, and choosing $h_k$ there kills those terms of $F_k$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a Hopf point, use the coordinates $(z, \bar z)$, with eigenvalues $i\omega$ and $-i\omega$. A monomial $z^p \bar z^q$ in the $\dot z$ equation is resonant when
$$
i\omega = (p - q)\, i\omega, \quad \text{that is} \quad p = q + 1 .
$$

The resonant terms are $z|z|^2, z|z|^4, \dots$: this is why the normal form of Theorem 3.5 keeps only $c_1 |z|^2 z$ at third order.

At a fold, the single eigenvalue $0$ makes every monomial resonant. The quadratic term survives, and the normal form is $\dot x = \beta + x^2$, after scaling by $f_{xx} \ne 0$.

### 3.5 Excitability classes of neurons

In 1948 Hodgkin sorted the axons of the crab *Carcinus* by their response to a constant current. Rinzel and Ermentrout (1989) explained his classes by the bifurcation through which the resting state gives way to repetitive firing.

::: def
[Definition 3.8 — Hodgkin's excitability classes]{.tag} A neuron is of *class 1* if repetitive firing can start at arbitrarily low frequency, and of *class 2* if the f–I curve jumps from $0$ to a positive frequency.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.9 — Onset of firing at a SNIC and at a Hopf point]{.tag}

1.  Suppose rest disappears in a saddle-node bifurcation at $I_c$ whose two equilibria lie on an invariant closed curve (a saddle-node on invariant circle, or SNIC). Then for $I > I_c$ the curve becomes a periodic orbit, and its frequency behaves like
$$
f \simeq \frac{\sqrt{c\, d\, (I - I_c)}}{\pi},
$$
where $c$ and $d$ are the coefficients of the reduced equation $\dot x = c\,(I - I_c) + d x^2$.
2.  If firing starts at a Hopf bifurcation, the frequency at onset is $\omega_0/2\pi > 0$, both in the supercritical and in the subcritical case.

Hence a SNIC produces class 1 excitability and a Hopf bifurcation class 2. The converse is not a theorem: a saddle-node whose equilibria do not lie on an invariant circle also gives class 2, since the neuron then jumps to a distant cycle of finite period (Izhikevich, 2007).

::: proof
*(1)* Near the ghost of the fold, the centre manifold reduction gives the normal form. The time to cross the bottleneck is
$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{c\,\delta + d x^2} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{c\, d\, \delta}}, \qquad \delta = I - I_c ,
$$
up to $O(1)$ corrections; the rest of the circle is crossed in a bounded time. The period diverges like $\delta^{-1/2}$.

*(2)* By Theorem 3.5, the period of the bifurcating cycle tends to $2\pi/\omega_0$. In the subcritical case, the large cycle reached after the jump also has a finite period. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron (Proposition 1.6) is exactly the SNIC normal form, with $f = \sqrt{I}/(\pi\tau)$. Hodgkin–Huxley and FitzHugh–Nagumo with standard parameters are class 2 (Examples 1.4 and 3.6). The Morris–Lecar model (1981) is a planar conductance-based model, with an instantaneous calcium current and a slower potassium current. It is class 1 or class 2 depending on its parameters, and many cortical pyramidal neurons behave as class 1.

A second distinction follows from the linearisation at rest. Close to a Hopf bifurcation the resting state is a stable focus: it produces damped subthreshold oscillations and responds best to inputs at its resonant frequency. Close to a saddle-node the resting state is a stable node, which simply integrates its inputs.

Izhikevich (2007) calls these neurons *resonators* and *integrators*. The difference is smooth, not topological (Theorem 2.8), yet it matters for timing.

### 3.6 Equivariant bifurcations

Neural fields on a ring or on the plane (ch. 5–6) are invariant under rotations, translations and reflections. Symmetry forces multiple eigenvalues, which are non-generic otherwise, and organises the solutions that bifurcate.

::: def
[Definition 3.10 — Equivariance, isotropy, fixed-point subspace]{.tag} Let a compact group $\Gamma$ act linearly and orthogonally on $\mathbb{R}^n$. The family $f(\cdot, \mu)$ is $\Gamma$-*equivariant* if, for all $\gamma \in \Gamma$,
$$
f(\gamma x, \mu) = \gamma f(x, \mu).
$$

The *isotropy subgroup* of $x$ and the *fixed-point subspace* of a subgroup $\Sigma$ are
$$
\Sigma_x = \{\gamma : \gamma x = x\}, \qquad \mathrm{Fix}(\Sigma) = \{x : \sigma x = x \text{ for all } \sigma \in \Sigma\}.
$$

Two facts follow at once.

-   If $x^*$ is an equilibrium, so is every $\gamma x^*$: equilibria come in group orbits.
-   $\mathrm{Fix}(\Sigma)$ is flow-invariant: for $x \in \mathrm{Fix}(\Sigma)$, $f(x) = f(\sigma x) = \sigma f(x)$, so $f(x) \in \mathrm{Fix}(\Sigma)$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.11 — Absolute irreducibility]{.tag} The action of $\Gamma$ is *absolutely irreducible* if the only linear maps commuting with every $\gamma$ are the multiples of the identity.

Then, at an equilibrium fixed by $\Gamma$, the Jacobian commutes with $\Gamma$, so $D_x f(0, \mu) = c(\mu)\, \mathrm{Id}$: all its eigenvalues are equal.

Example: $\mathrm{O}(2)$, rotations and reflections, acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is absolutely irreducible; the rotations $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ alone are not, since they commute with each other.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.12 — Equivariant branching lemma (Vanderbauwhede; Cicogna)]{.tag} Let $\Gamma$ act absolutely irreducibly on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with $f(0, \mu) = 0$ and $D_x f(0, \mu) = c(\mu)\,\mathrm{Id}$, where $c(0) = 0$ and $c'(0) \ne 0$.

If $\Sigma$ is an isotropy subgroup with $\dim \mathrm{Fix}(\Sigma) = 1$, a unique branch of equilibria with symmetry $\Sigma$ bifurcates from $(0, 0)$.

::: proof
Restrict $f$ to the invariant line $\mathrm{Fix}(\Sigma) = \mathbb{R} e$. Writing $x = t e$ gives a scalar equation $\dot t = g(t, \mu)$ with $g(0, \mu) = 0$.

Moreover $g_t(0, 0) = c(0) = 0$ and $g_{t\mu}(0, 0) = c'(0) \ne 0$.

As in Proposition 3.3, write $g = t\, k(t, \mu)$ with $k(0,0) = 0$ and $k_\mu(0, 0) \ne 0$. The implicit function theorem solves $k = 0$ as $\mu = m(t)$: this is the branch. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The case used in ch. 6 is $\mathrm{O}(2)$ acting on $\mathbb{C} \simeq \mathbb{R}^2$ by rotations $z \mapsto e^{i\phi} z$ and the reflection $z \mapsto \bar z$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.13 — O(2)-equivariant vector fields]{.tag} Every smooth $\mathrm{O}(2)$-equivariant map $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ has the form
$$
f(z) = p(|z|^2)\, z, \qquad p \text{ real-valued and smooth} .
$$

Consequently, when $p(0, \mu)$ changes sign at $\mu = 0$ with non-zero speed and $\partial_\rho p(0, 0) \ne 0$, a *circle* of equilibria $|z|^2 = \rho(\mu)$ bifurcates from $0$ on one side of $\mu = 0$ (a pitchfork of revolution). Each equilibrium on it has a zero eigenvalue along the circle.

::: proof
For $r > 0$, rotation equivariance gives $f(r e^{i\phi}) = e^{i\phi} f(r)$, and reflection equivariance gives $f(r) = f(\bar r) = \overline{f(r)}$, so $f(r)$ is real.

Rotation by $\pi$ gives $f(-r) = -f(r)$, so $f(r)/r$ extends to an even smooth function of $r$, hence (Whitney) a smooth function $p$ of $r^2$.

Then $f(z) = p(|z|^2)\, z$ for every $z$.

The non-zero equilibria solve $p(\rho, \mu) = 0$ with $\rho = |z|^2 > 0$. Since $\partial_\rho p(0, 0) \ne 0$, the implicit function theorem gives $\rho = \rho(\mu)$, with $\rho'(0) \ne 0$, which is positive on one side of $\mu = 0$.

The zero eigenvalue comes from differentiating the identity $f(e^{i\phi} z^*) = 0$ in $\phi$: the tangent vector $i z^*$ to the circle is in the kernel. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The isotropy subgroup of a real point $z = r > 0$ is the reflection, whose fixed-point subspace $\mathbb{R}$ is one-dimensional, as Theorem 3.12 requires. Without the reflection, $p$ may be complex, and the circle of equilibria becomes a circle of rotating waves.
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Local bifurcations of equilibria need a non-hyperbolic equilibrium; generically a zero eigenvalue (fold) or an imaginary pair (Hopf).
-   Normal forms: fold $\dot x = \beta \pm x^2$, transcritical $\dot x = \beta x - x^2$, pitchfork $\dot x = \beta x \mp x^3$, Hopf $\dot z = (\alpha + i\omega) z + c_1|z|^2 z$.
-   The sign of the first Lyapunov coefficient separates soft (supercritical) from hard (subcritical) onset; FitzHugh–Nagumo and Hodgkin–Huxley are subcritical.
-   Centre manifold reduction plus Poincaré normal forms reduce any dimension to the critical directions; resonances decide which terms remain.
-   A saddle-node on an invariant circle gives class 1 firing (f grows like the square root of I − I_c); a Hopf bifurcation gives class 2 firing (finite frequency at onset). These are the two main routes, not the only ones.
-   Symmetry forces multiple eigenvalues; one-dimensional fixed-point subspaces give branches (equivariant branching lemma); O(2) symmetry gives circles of equilibria.
:::

## 4. The role of noise {#ch4}

Recorded in vivo, cortical neurons fire irregularly: the coefficient of variation of their interspike intervals is often close to 1, the value of a Poisson process (Softky and Koch, 1993). Channels open at random, synapses release transmitter at random, and each neuron is bombarded by thousands of inputs. This chapter builds the stochastic calculus needed to model this variability and computes the firing rate of a noisy neuron in closed form.

### 4.1 Brownian motion

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Brownian motion]{.tag} A real process $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a standard Brownian motion if $B_0 = 0$, its paths are continuous, and its increments over disjoint intervals are independent, with
$$
B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, t - s), \qquad 0 \le s \le t .
$$

It exists (Wiener, 1923), and it is the scaling limit of random walks: if $S_n$ is a sum of $n$ i.i.d. steps of variance 1, the process $S_{\lfloor nt \rfloor}/\sqrt{n}$ converges in law to $B$ (Donsker).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Quadratic variation]{.tag} Let $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_K = t$ be partitions of $[0, t]$ whose mesh tends to $0$. Then, in $L^2$,
$$
\sum_{k} \big(B_{t_{k+1}} - B_{t_k}\big)^2 \longrightarrow t .
$$

::: proof
Each square has mean $\Delta t_k$ and variance $2\Delta t_k^2$, and the squares are independent. The sum has mean $t$ and variance
$$
2 \sum_k \Delta t_k^2 \le 2t \max_k \Delta t_k \to 0 .
$$

Convergence in $L^2$ to $t$ follows. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A continuous path with non-zero quadratic variation has infinite total variation on every interval. Therefore $\int H\, dB$ cannot be defined path by path as a Stieltjes integral; Itô's construction uses the $L^2$ structure instead.

The heuristic rule $(dB_t)^2 = dt$ summarises Proposition 4.2.

### 4.2 The Itô integral and stochastic differential equations

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Itô integral]{.tag} Let $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ be the filtration of $B$. For a simple adapted process $H = \sum_k H_k \mathbb{1}_{(t_k, t_{k+1}]}$, with $H_k$ bounded and $\mathcal{F}_{t_k}$-measurable, set
$$
\int_0^t H_s\, dB_s = \sum_k H_k\, \big(B_{t_{k+1} \wedge t} - B_{t_k \wedge t}\big).
$$

It is a centred martingale and satisfies the Itô isometry
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\int_0^t H_s\, dB_s\Big)^2\Big] = \mathbb{E}\int_0^t H_s^2\, ds .
$$

By density, the integral extends to all adapted $H$ with $\mathbb{E}\int_0^t H^2 < \infty$, keeping both properties.

*Why the isometry holds*: in the square of the sum, a cross term $H_j H_k \Delta B_j \Delta B_k$ with $j < k$ has zero mean, because $\Delta B_k$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{t_k}$. A diagonal term has mean $\mathbb{E}[H_k^2]\, \Delta t_k$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Existence and uniqueness for SDEs]{.tag} Let $b$ and $\sigma$ be globally Lipschitz on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $X_0$ square-integrable, independent of $B$. The equation
$$
dX_t = b(X_t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t)\, dB_t
$$
has a unique continuous adapted solution, and $\mathbb{E}\sup_{t \le T} |X_t|^2 < \infty$ for every $T$.

::: proof
*Existence*: define the Picard iterates and their distances,
$$
X^{n+1}_t = X_0 + \int_0^t b(X^n_s)\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma(X^n_s)\, dB_s, \qquad D_n(t) = \mathbb{E}\sup_{s \le t}|X^{n+1}_s - X^n_s|^2 .
$$

Doob's maximal inequality, the Itô isometry and the Lipschitz bounds give
$$
D_n(t) \le C \int_0^t D_{n-1}(s)\, ds, \quad \text{hence} \quad D_n(t) \le D_0(T)\, \frac{(Ct)^n}{n!} .
$$

This is summable, so $X^n$ converges uniformly on $[0, T]$ in $L^2$ to a solution.

*Uniqueness*: for two solutions $X$ and $Y$, the same estimate applied to $\delta(t) = \mathbb{E}\sup_{s \le t} |X_s - Y_s|^2$ gives
$$
\delta(t) \le C \int_0^t \delta(s)\, ds ,
$$
and Grönwall's lemma (Lemma 0.2) gives $\delta = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Simulations use the Euler–Maruyama scheme, which replaces $dB$ by a Gaussian increment of variance $\Delta t$:
$$
X_{k+1} = X_k + b(X_k)\, \Delta t + \sigma(X_k)\, \sqrt{\Delta t}\; \xi_k, \qquad \xi_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \text{ i.i.d.}
$$

Its strong error is of order $\sqrt{\Delta t}$ in general (Kloeden and Platen, 1992).

### 4.3 Itô's formula and the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Itô's formula]{.tag} Let $X$ solve $dX = b\, dt + \sigma\, dB$, and let $F(t, x)$ be once differentiable in time and twice in space, with continuous derivatives. Then
$$
dF(t, X_t) = \Big(\partial_t F + b\, \partial_x F + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\, \partial_{xx} F\Big)\, dt + \sigma\, \partial_x F\; dB_t .
$$

*Proof sketch*: write $F(t, X_t) - F(0, X_0)$ as a telescoping sum over a partition and expand each term to second order. The sum of $\frac12 \partial_{xx}F\, (\Delta X)^2$ converges to $\frac12\int \partial_{xx}F\, \sigma^2\, dt$ by Proposition 4.2; higher-order terms vanish in the limit.
::::

The extra term $\frac12 \sigma^2 \partial_{xx} F$ is the whole difference with ordinary calculus. For example, $d(B_t^2) = 2B_t\, dB_t + dt$, so $B_t^2 - t$ is a martingale.

::: ex
[Example 4.6 — The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process]{.tag} The free membrane potential of a leaky neuron driven by white noise is
$$
\tau\, dX_t = (\mu - X_t)\, dt + \sigma \sqrt{\tau}\; dB_t .
$$

Itô's formula applied to $e^{t/\tau} X_t$ removes the drift and gives the explicit solution
$$
X_t = \mu + (X_0 - \mu)\, e^{-t/\tau} + \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}} \int_0^t e^{-(t-s)/\tau}\, dB_s .
$$

-   The mean relaxes to $\mu$ with time constant $\tau$.
-   By the Itô isometry, the variance is $\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau}\int_0^t e^{-2(t-s)/\tau}\, ds$.
-   It tends to $\sigma^2/2$, and the stationary law is $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/2)$.

With $\tau = 20$ ms and $\sigma = 5$ mV, the stationary standard deviation of the potential is about 3.5 mV.
:::

### 4.4 The Fokker–Planck equation and first-passage times

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Fokker–Planck equation]{.tag} Let $X$ solve $dX = b(X)\, dt + \sigma(X)\, dB$ in dimension 1, and suppose $X_t$ has a smooth density $p(t, x)$. Then
$$
\partial_t p = -\partial_x \big(b\, p\big) + \frac{1}{2}\, \partial_{xx}\big(\sigma^2 p\big).
$$

::: proof
For a smooth compactly supported test function $\varphi$, Itô's formula and the zero mean of the stochastic integral give
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\, \mathbb{E}\varphi(X_t) = \mathbb{E}\Big[b\, \varphi'(X_t) + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\, \varphi''(X_t)\Big].
$$

Write both sides as integrals against $p(t, \cdot)$ and integrate by parts on the right; since $\varphi$ is arbitrary, the densities agree. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The operator $L\varphi = b\varphi' + \frac12\sigma^2\varphi''$ is the *generator* of $X$. In the stationary regime with zero flux, the Fokker–Planck equation integrates once and gives
$$
p_\infty(x) \propto \frac{1}{\sigma^2(x)}\, \exp\Big(\int^x \frac{2 b(y)}{\sigma^2(y)}\, dy\Big).
$$

For the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process this is the Gaussian of Example 4.6.

A neuron fires when its potential first reaches the threshold. The mean time to get there solves an ordinary differential equation.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.8 — Mean first-passage time]{.tag} Let $X$ be a one-dimensional diffusion with $\sigma > 0$, started at $x < \theta$, and $T(x) = \mathbb{E}_x[\inf\{t : X_t = \theta\}]$. Under growth conditions at $-\infty$ that make the lower boundary non-attracting, $T$ solves
$$
b\, T' + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\, T'' = -1 \ \text{ on } (-\infty, \theta), \qquad T(\theta) = 0 .
$$

With $\psi(y) = \exp\big(\int^y 2b/\sigma^2\big)$, its solution is
$$
T(x) = \int_x^\theta \frac{1}{\psi(y)} \int_{-\infty}^{y} \frac{2\, \psi(z)}{\sigma^2(z)}\, dz\, dy .
$$

::: proof
*Equation* (Dynkin's argument). Apply Itô's formula to $T(X_t)$ up to the stopped time $\tau_\theta \wedge t$, take expectations, and use $LT = -1$:
$$
\mathbb{E}_x\, T(X_{\tau_\theta \wedge t}) = T(x) - \mathbb{E}_x[\tau_\theta \wedge t].
$$
Let $t \to \infty$. The right-hand side converges by monotone convergence. On the left, $T(X_{\tau_\theta \wedge t}) \to T(\theta) = 0$, and the growth conditions at $-\infty$ give the uniform integrability needed to exchange limit and expectation.

*Solution.* The equation reads $(\psi T')' = -2\psi/\sigma^2$. Integrate from $-\infty$, where $\psi T' \to 0$, then from $x$ to $\theta$ using $T(\theta) = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 4.5 Noisy integrate-and-fire neurons

Suppose a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron receives $C$ independent Poisson inputs of rate $\nu$, each making the potential jump by $J$. Then $dV = -V\,dt/\tau + J\, dN_t$, where $N$ is Poisson with rate $C\nu$.

If $J$ is small and $C\nu$ large, the input is approximated by its mean and its Gaussian fluctuations (the diffusion approximation). The result is $\tau\, dV = (\mu - V)\, dt + \sigma\sqrt{\tau}\, dB$ below threshold, with
$$
\mu = C J \nu \tau, \qquad \sigma^2 = C J^2 \nu \tau .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.9 — Firing rate of the noisy leaky integrate-and-fire neuron (Siegert formula)]{.tag} Let $\tau\, dV = (\mu - V)\, dt + \sigma\sqrt{\tau}\, dB$ below the threshold $\theta$, with reset to $V_r$ and refractory period $\tau_{\text{ref}}$. The stationary firing rate $\nu_{\text{out}}$ is given by
$$
\frac{1}{\nu_{\text{out}}} = \tau_{\text{ref}} + \tau \sqrt{\pi} \int_{(V_r - \mu)/\sigma}^{(\theta - \mu)/\sigma} e^{u^2}\, \big(1 + \mathrm{erf}\, u\big)\, du .
$$

::: proof
The interspike intervals are i.i.d., each equal to $\tau_{\text{ref}}$ plus a first-passage time from $V_r$ to $\theta$. By the renewal theorem the rate is the inverse of the mean interval, so it suffices to compute $T(V_r)$.

Apply Proposition 4.8 with $b(v) = (\mu - v)/\tau$ and noise intensity $\sigma^2/\tau$. Then $2b/(\sigma^2/\tau) = 2(\mu - v)/\sigma^2$ and $\psi(y) = e^{-(y - \mu)^2/\sigma^2}$.

Substituting $u = (y - \mu)/\sigma$ and $s = (z - \mu)/\sigma$:
$$
T(V_r) = 2\tau \int_{(V_r - \mu)/\sigma}^{(\theta - \mu)/\sigma} e^{u^2} \int_{-\infty}^{u} e^{-s^2}\, ds\, du ,
$$
and the inner integral is $\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}(1 + \mathrm{erf}\, u)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.10 — Siegert formula against simulation]{.tag} We take the values of Brunel (2000): $\tau = 20$ ms, $\theta = 20$ mV, $V_r = 10$ mV, $\tau_{\text{ref}} = 2$ ms. The mean input $\mu = 18$ mV stays below threshold, so a noiseless neuron would never fire.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.special import erfcx

tau, theta, Vr, tref = 20.0, 20.0, 10.0, 2.0      # ms, mV (values of Brunel, 2000)
mu, sigma = 18.0, 5.0                              # mean input and noise amplitude (mV)

# Siegert formula; e^{u^2} (1 + erf u) = erfcx(-u) avoids overflow
integral = quad(lambda u: erfcx(-u), (Vr - mu) / sigma, (theta - mu) / sigma)[0]
nu_theory = 1000.0 / (tref + tau * np.sqrt(np.pi) * integral)

# Euler-Maruyama for tau dV = (mu - V) dt + sigma sqrt(tau) dB, N neurons in parallel
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, dt, T, T0 = 1000, 0.02, 600.0, 100.0           # T0: discarded transient (ms)
V = np.full(N, Vr); ref = np.zeros(N); spikes = 0
for k in range(int(T / dt)):
    active = ref <= 0
    V[active] += (mu - V[active]) * dt / tau \
                 + sigma * np.sqrt(dt / tau) * rng.standard_normal(active.sum())
    ref -= dt
    fired = V >= theta
    if k * dt > T0:
        spikes += fired.sum()
    V[fired] = Vr; ref[fired] = tref
nu_sim = 1000 * spikes / (N * (T - T0))
print(f"Siegert: {nu_theory:.2f} Hz   Euler-Maruyama: {nu_sim:.2f} Hz")
```

The formula gives 19.62 Hz and the simulation 19.34 Hz. The residual gap of about 1.5 % comes from threshold crossings missed between two time steps; it shrinks with $\Delta t$.

Noise alone makes the neuron fire at about 20 Hz with a subthreshold mean input.
:::

The density of the potential of a noisy integrate-and-fire neuron solves the Fokker–Planck equation of Proposition 4.7 on $(-\infty, \theta)$, with an absorbing boundary at $\theta$. The outgoing flux at $\theta$ is the firing rate, and it is reinjected at $V_r$.
